seoTitle.en: Heroes of the High Andes: the real animals behind The Circle of Paws

description.en: Fur so thick fleas can't live in it, a bird that sleeps clinging to cave walls, and poop that turns mountains green. Real Andes animal facts for kids.

intro.en: Every animal in The Circle of Paws is real. Here is how they live, what they eat and the true secrets behind the story.

name.en: The puna, high in the Andes

intro.en: Killa lives on the puna, a high, cold grassland across Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina, mostly above 3,200 metres.

title.en: Shorts at lunch, snowsuit at bedtime

text.en: Afternoons can reach about 25 °C, then most nights drop below freezing. The swing between day and night can be as big as 45 °C. Every animal in this book has a trick to survive it.
In summer, the rain on the puna often falls as hail. The hailstorm in the story is real puna weather.
Kinti's twisted tree is a queñua (ken-YOO-ah). Some grow above 5,000 metres. Its name, Polylepis, means "many layers": its red bark peels in thin sheets, like paper.
Some queñuas take more than 100 years to grow half an inch wider. The tree in the story might be older than your great-grandparents.
The steps on the hillsides are farming terraces called andenes. Each step has its own little climate, so families can grow different crops on one hill. Farmers still use them today.
A real puna where wild vicuñas live, 3,700 to 4,300 metres up. It's where villagers hold the chaccu every year.

areaNote.en: Yellow: the four countries of the puna.

job.en: The fastest helper on the mountain

superpower.en: The thickest fur of any land animal

value.en: 22–38 cm, plus a 7–15 cm bushy tail
0.5–0.8 kg, about a loaf of bread
About 10 years wild, 20+ as a pet
Grass and seeds, sometimes insects
Rock cracks, 3,000–5,000 m up
Dusk and night
Endangered

text.en: Killa's alarm clock goes off at sunset. Chinchillas sleep through the bright day in a rock crack and wake when the light goes soft. Breakfast is a salad of grass and seeds. A tasty insect or a bird egg? A chinchilla isn't fussy.
No soft burrows here. Chinchillas live in cracks and holes between rocks on bare, dry mountainsides. Hard walls, a great view, no lawn to mow.
Wild colonies can hold more than 100 chinchillas. The females are bigger than the males, and they are the bosses.
Mom carries her babies for about 111 days, very long for a small rodent, and usually has two or three, about twice a year. The kits are born with fur on and eyes open.
You grow one hair from each tiny hole in your skin. A chinchilla grows 50 to 60. Its coat is the densest of any land mammal; only the sea otter beats it.
Chinchilla fur is so thick it can't dry, so they never bathe in water. They flip and roll in fine dust instead, and in the wild, volcanic ash.
Grabbed by a predator? A chinchilla lets go of a clump of fur and runs, leaving the hunter with a mouthful of fluff. Then it bounces away: chinchillas can jump 1.8 metres.
Chinchillas can't sweat. They let out extra heat through their big ears.

storyVsReal.en: Real chinchillas are quick, springy jumpers, just like Killa. But a real one would be fast asleep at noon. Killa is a daytime chinchilla, just for the story.

job.en: The tall, patient friend who keeps offering

superpower.en: The finest wool in the world

value.en: 70–110 cm at the shoulder, the smallest of the camel family
35–65 kg, about a grown-up
About 20 years wild
Short grasses, and a drink every day
Open grassland, 3,200–4,800 m up
Peru's national animal
Least Concern: a comeback story

text.en: Grass. And more grass. Vicuñas nibble short mountain grasses and, unlike most of their camel cousins, need a drink of water every single day.
A vicuña family eats in one patch all day, then walks to a separate, higher spot to sleep. A dining room and a bedroom, on different parts of the mountain.
A family is one dad with a group of moms, often 5 to 15, and their babies. Dad guards the territory all year and calls an alarm when danger comes, so Mom and baby can eat in peace. Sounds like Sami.
Mom carries one baby for almost a year, 330 to 350 days. It nurses for up to ten months and is grown up at about one. Then Dad sends the young ones off to find their own way.
One vicuña hair is about 12 microns wide, thinner than the finest cashmere and far thinner than yours. That's how Sami stays warm on freezing nights.
Vicuñas once numbered in the millions. Poachers hunted them for their wool, and by the mid-1960s only about 6,000 were left in Peru.

Andean villages brought back the chaccu: every June, people join hands across the mountains, gently gather the wild vicuñas, shear a little wool and let every one go free. Today Peru has over 200,000.
Vicuña families share one bathroom: a dung pile. On bare rock left by melting glaciers, these piles help plants grow about a hundred years sooner.
A vicuña's bottom front teeth never stop growing, like a rodent's. No other hoofed animal has teeth like that. Sami and Killa have more in common than you'd think.

storyVsReal.en: Real vicuñas don't wear ear tassels: Sami's red tassel makes him easy to spot on every page. And a real vicuña would be out with his whole family.

caption.fr: Une vigogne sauvage dans les Andes

job.en: The tiny bird who thinks she's too small to help

superpower.en: Survives freezing nights by nearly switching off

value.en: 13–15 cm, beak to tail
About 8 g, a little more than a loonie
Not known: nobody has tracked wild hillstars long enough
Flower nectar, with insects on the side
Rocky valleys and grassland, 2,400–5,000 m up
Least Concern, a common puna bird

text.en: Sugar! Hillstars drink nectar from tough mountain shrubs and little cushion cacti, and snatch insects for protein. Most hummingbirds hover to eat; hillstars usually perch on the flower. Saving energy, even at dinner.

title.en: The coziest nest on the mountain

text.en: Mom builds a woolly cup up to 8 cm deep from plant fibres and wool, often camelid wool from Sami's family. She sticks it to a rock wall with spider silk, facing the morning sun. A circle of helping, in real life!
Mom holds the territory, builds the nest and raises the chicks alone while Dad roams. She sits on two eggs for 20 days, and the chicks fly about 38 days after hatching.

title.en: The bird that almost switches off

text.en: To survive freezing nights, a hillstar lets its body cool to about 7 °C, close to a fridge, and sinks into a deep sleep called torpor. It was the first hummingbird proven to do it.
Hillstars spend the night in caves, clinging to the rock and propped on their tails. When scientists checked, every hillstar sleeping in the caves was a female. Kinti in her rock nook: true to life.
Hail can stop a hillstar from feeding all day: then a 15-hour fast and a freezing night on an empty tank. Scientists call their survival remarkable. Tiny Kinti is tougher than she thinks.

storyVsReal.en: Only the male hillstar has the shiny green throat; females have a pale, speckled one. We gave Kinti the sparkle anyway. Can your child spot the change?

job.en: The neighbours on the sunny rocks

value.en: A rabbit with a long, curly, bushy tail
Up to 3 kg, four times a chinchilla
Up to about 19 years in zoos
Grasses, mosses and lichens
Cracks under rocky outcrops
Day, busiest at sunrise and sunset

text.en: Mostly grasses, plus mosses and even crusty lichens off the rocks. Like chinchillas, they sit up straight to eat. Very good table manners.
Each small family has its own crack under the rocks, and many families live side by side in a loose colony.
Mom carries her baby for about four months and usually has just one or two. The little striped one in our story is extra precious.
They look like rabbits, but viscachas belong to the chinchilla family. Killa and her neighbours are real relatives.
After a freezing night, viscachas sit on rocks to soak up the sun, like grumpy grandpas on beach chairs.
The Andean mountain cat hunts viscachas. So one always keeps watch, and a high whistle sends everyone diving for the rocks. Looking out for each other: that's a circle too.

storyVsReal.en: Chinchillas work the night shift and viscachas the day shift, so in real life the neighbours mostly take turns on the same rocks.

caption.en: A real viscacha on a sunny rock
caption.fr: Une vraie viscache sur un rocher au soleil

job.en: The little family with big hearts

value.en: 22–27 cm, and no tail at all
295–390 g, about a can of soup
Pets about 5–6 years; wild ones aren't well studied
Herbs and grasses of mountain meadows
Rocky, grassy places with secret runways
Mostly dawn and dusk

text.en: Wild guinea pigs eat the herbs and grasses of mountain meadows, at ground level, all day long, to keep their busy little bodies going.
They wear secret runways through thick plants to scurry out of sight, and in some places live in burrows with several doors. Very handy when someone hungry comes knocking.
Guinea pigs live in small herds, and some dads help groom and play with the babies. Moms have one to four at a time, grown up at about two months.

title.en: Every pet guinea pig came from here

text.en: People in the Andes tamed guinea pigs thousands of years ago, from a wild ancestor like this one. A pet guinea pig's family tree starts on Killa's mountain.
Most baby rodents are born bald and blind. Guinea-pig babies arrive with fur, open eyes and teeth, and nibble solid food right away.
Guinea pigs can't make their own vitamin C, so they get it from plants. Humans can't either. Eat your veggies!
Big eyes, big ears and a sharp nose spot danger early. When it comes, the whole group scatters in every direction to confuse the hunter.

storyVsReal.en: Real wild guinea pigs are plain sandy-brown, just as we painted them. The swirly colours of pets came later, from people breeding them.

text.en: Find a loonie, a can of soup and a loaf of bread. Which hero weighs the same as each?
A hand in the fridge for three seconds. Brrr! That's how cold a sleeping hillstar gets.
Wrap ten sheets of tissue round a tube, then peel one: a queñua losing an old coat.
Pass a cushion hand to hand, like the villagers at a chaccu, and the animals in the story.
Flip through the book: find Kinti's sparkly throat, Sami's tassel and Killa awake at noon.

q.en: Are the animals in The Circle of Paws real?

a.en: Yes. Chinchillas, vicuñas, mountain viscachas, wild guinea pigs and Andean hillstars all live in the Andes today. We changed a few small things for the story, and each hero tells you what.
Wild chinchillas are, after years of fur hunting. Pet chinchillas are bred in captivity.

q.en: What's the difference between a vicuña, a llama and an alpaca?

a.en: Llamas and alpacas are tame animals that people raise. Vicuñas are wild, and DNA research suggests alpacas descend from them.
A very deep, cold sleep that saves energy. The Andean hillstar was the first hummingbird shown to use it.
